Series::CalcAccessor::options¶

Back to Series::CalcAccessor API Reference

Signature¶

const Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions&
Series::CalcAccessor::options() const noexcept

What It Returns¶

options() returns a read-only reference to the policy currently bound to a calculus accessor. The root member x.calc starts with default options; x.calc(custom) returns a lightweight accessor containing a copy of custom. Inspecting the copy is useful when a configured accessor is passed through generic code and the eventual terminal operation needs to report or branch on its policy.

options() does not validate a policy by itself. Validation belongs to the terminal method because fields have operation-specific meaning. For example, order=0 is valid for diff() but invalid for antidiff(), and a missing lower matters only to the no-bound antidiff(fn) overload.

AntidiffOptions is a type alias for CalcOptions; it does not define a second policy object.

Precedence¶

Bound options provide defaults. A terminal argument replaces the corresponding field for that call:

  • configured.diff(fn, n) uses n, not configured.options().order;

  • configured.antidiff(fn, a) uses a, not configured.options().lower;

  • configured.antidiff(fn, a, other) uses other for the entire call.

The original configured accessor is unchanged by all three forms. This makes a configured accessor safe to reuse across calls with occasional overrides.

Examples¶

Example 1. Bind and inspect an integration policy.

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.lower = 0.0;
options.intervals = 32;
options.adaptive = false;

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0});
auto configured = x.calc(options);
const auto& policy = configured.options();

std::cout << "lower=" << *policy.lower << "\n";
std::cout << "intervals=" << policy.intervals << "\n";
std::cout << "adaptive=" << std::boolalpha << policy.adaptive << "\n";

Output¶

lower=0
intervals=32
adaptive=false

Example 2. The bound lower endpoint is used when omitted; an explicit endpoint overrides it without changing the stored policy.

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.lower = 0.0;
options.intervals = 32;
options.adaptive = false;

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0});
auto configured = x.calc(options);
auto square = [](const pluss::Series& t) { return t.square(); };

std::cout << "bound=" << configured.antidiff(square) << "\n";
std::cout << "override=" << configured.antidiff(square, 1.0) << "\n";
std::cout << "still_bound_to=" << *configured.options().lower << "\n";

Output¶

bound=pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.041666667, 0.33333333, 1.125, 2.6666667]
override=pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.29166667, 0, 0.79166667, 2.3333333]
still_bound_to=0

Example 3. A bound derivative order is the default, while an explicit order changes one call only.

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.order = 2;

auto x = pluss::make_series(0.5);
auto configured = x.calc(options);
auto sine = [](const pluss::Series& z) { return z.sin(); };

std::cout << std::setprecision(10);
std::cout << "bound_second=" << configured.diff(sine).item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "explicit_first=" << configured.diff(sine, 1).item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "stored_order=" << configured.options().order << "\n";

Output¶

bound_second=-0.4794255386
explicit_first=0.8775825619
stored_order=2

Example 4. One policy can define a second antiderivative completely, including its anchor and both lower-bound conditions.

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.order = 2;
options.lower = 0.0;
options.initial = {2.0, 3.0};
options.adaptive = false;
options.intervals = 32;

auto upper = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0});
auto configured = upper.calc(options);
auto result = configured.antidiff(
    [](const pluss::Series& t) { return t.mul(0.0).add(1.0); });

std::cout << result << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[3.625, 5.5, 10]

Ownership And Lifetime¶

The configured accessor owns its option copy but only borrows the receiver. Mutating the original CalcOptions after x.calc(options) does not alter the configured accessor. The reference returned by options() remains valid only as long as that accessor object remains alive; do not retain a reference taken from a temporary such as x.calc(options).options().

Failure Modes¶

options() itself is noexcept. Invalid values are diagnosed when a terminal method consumes them. See diff for derivative validation and antidiff for integration validation.
